utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. If I could remind you, Dr. Gashi, of the affirmation you made at the commencement of your evidence, which still applies. Mr. Powles.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Gashi.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Not very much more for you, you'll be pleased to hear. The first question is this: It's right that you never saw Qerqiz wearing a mask in Lapusnik during the time that you were there, did you?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: You stated yesterday that you heard from others that Qerqiz would interview prospective soldiers in Lapusnik. So just to clarify, that's not something you had personal knowledge of, that's something that you were told and that you heard from other people.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard from other people. Personally I didn't have knowledge about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Did you also hear from other people that Ymer Alushani would also interview prospective soldiers in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: To make it clear at the outset, Mr. Musliu accepts that he was one of the commanders in Lapusnik but not the only commander in Lapusnik. When you met with Howard Tucker, the prosecutor -- the Prosecution investigator in September of 2003, it's right, isn't it, Dr. Gashi, that you said you had no personal knowledge about who commanded the KLA in Lapusnik. That's right, isn't it, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I explained yesterday during my testimony the reason why I said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: You also stated in your testimony yesterday that Ymer Alushani introduced you to one of the leaders of the KLA by the pseudonym Qerqizi. If the Prosecution would like the reference for that, it's page 34, lines 9 and 10 of the transcript. So yesterday, Dr. Gashi, you said that Ymer Alushani introduced you to one of the leaders of the KLA in Lapusnik. It's right, isn't it, Doctor, that you treated soldiers from other units in your clinic in Lapusnik? When I say "other units," I mean units other than Celiku 3.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my recollection, I have not treated soldiers of other units during my time in Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Now, this may be something that you're not able to help with, Doctor, not being a military man yourself, but it's right, isn't it, that there were other units other than Celiku 3 based in Lapusnik, namely the Pelumbi unit and the Gurri unit?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible, but when we treated soldiers, we didn't know to which unit they belonged. For us, they were patients, not soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Yes. But what I'm asking you, Doctor, is were you aware of the Pelumbi and the Gurri unit being in Lapusnik? It may be something that you weren't aware of, but if it is, then you should say so.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have knowledge of this. As I said yesterday, our goal was to offer medical services, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: May I go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Powles.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I don't know if Mr. Khan had questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I knew if I waited long enough you would forget about me. Perhaps just one question of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Dr. Gashi, my name is Khan and I represent Fatmir Limaj. You have earlier said that you know Mr. Ferat Sopi; is that right? Ferat Sopi.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And it's correct, isn't it, that he worked as a technician, helping you in the makeshift hospital in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He worked for a short period because he had moved his family out from Lapusnik. He came from time to time, but he didn't stay for longer periods.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Are you aware that on the 25th of July KLA soldiers from many different units came down to assist and help in the fight against the forces from the former Yugoslavia, the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very possible that other soldiers were there as well, because that was a key position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: No doubt the 25th of July was a very hectic day, and no doubt you were very busy. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Usually, as I mentioned yesterday during my testimony, that on this date we moved our supplies from that clinic to another house which was safer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Can you remember seeing Fatmir Limaj come to your makeshift clinic in the afternoon of the 25th of July? Do you remember that or not?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Do you remember him being in a very bad state, and if it may help you, do you remember him having very swollen, red, and watering eyes?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Khan. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have no questions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Dr. Gashi, you will be pleased to know that that concludes the questions that will be asked of you. The Tribunal is grateful that you have come and assisted in this trial, and you are now able to return to your place of living. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness is ready to testify, but before we have the next witness, the Prosecution has a few additional exhibits and statements to admit into evidence. Only because I'm at the microphone I'll go first and do a couple and then Colin -- Mr. Colin Black will do a few more. The first concerns the document which I'll ask, with the assistance of the usher, be distributed to the -- it has not been provided to the Chamber or to the parties, but if it could be provided now. That is to say the parties -- the Defence is aware of this, but -- to the Court, to everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that this document, which is ERN U 008 -- sorry, U 0008352, one-page document and the translation, be given a number with the following agreement or stipulation: That is that this document was provided to the Office of the Prosecutor by the government of Serbia along with a collection of other documents on or about 11 October 2001. By letter dated 23 June 2004, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Serbia and Montenegro represented that this document was found in the village of Likovac by Serbian MUP forces sometime between 3 August and 7 August 1998. This is an agreement, a stipulation that's been reached with the Defence, and on this basis it's been agreed with the Defence that the document will be go into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Let me be clearer: Are you saying that those facts that you've recited are also agreed?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see. And is it agreed that this witness was two years old when this statement was made?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I believe that other evidence -- on the basis of other evidence we'll be able to indicate that the -- that there's an error, that the two numbers are transposed in that -- in that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps born 1969 instead of 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour. And there is other evidence that is already in the record on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So this is a motion pursuant to Rule 92 bis, is it, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it is 92 bis because -- I think it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Simply the document that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, and I think it can go in as an agreed fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see no sign of dissent from your motion, so the document will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P218.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: For the next matter I have to deal with I have another -- I will require again the assistance of the usher in distributing a document that the Prosecution and the Defence would like jointly to admit into evidence. This is simply -- this is a -- this document originates from an OSCE report called "As Seen, As Told," and all it is is a name list of villages in Kosovo. The first half is the names of the villages in Serbian -- in the Serbian language are listed alphabetically, and the corresponding Albanian name and municipality are then provided, so the second half of the document goes the other way. The names in the Albanian language are listed alphabetically and the corresponding Serbian name of the Serbian village is then provided. And this -- the parties thought that this should be provided to the Court and made an exhibit simply as an aide in tracking the evidence and following the villages and keeping track, because sometimes different names are used for the same village. So if this could be given -- I don't know if there is a possibility of a joint exhibit number or a Court number or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Why not a Prosecution number, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Prosecution Exhibit P219.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And now I cede the floor to Mr. Black who has some other statements and documents to put into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. As Mr. Whiting indicated, just a few more things. I believe Mr. Younis distributed before the start of court a binder - a thin binder, he says - labelled "Rule 92 bis witnesses and expert materials" with today's date, the 12th of April, 2005. Your Honour, I propose to go through a similar drill to that which we performed last Monday, which is essentially for me to go through the tabs and ask for an exhibit number for each. But before I do that, by way of introduction I would just note that yesterday we filed the Prosecution's fifth motion for admission pursuant to Rule 92 bis, as well as a motion for protective measures with regard to 92 bis witnesses. Perhaps it's easiest to deal with those motions as they relate to specific witnesses as we did last week but I just mention it so that the Court is aware. Should I begin with the first tab?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, the materials behind tab 1 are 92 bis materials for Witness L97. This is a witness for whom we've agreed with the Defence, subject to some redactions, to have his evidence admitted in written form. This evidence is subject to a motion to add him to the witness list and to admit his -- his statements pursuant to 92 bis which the Prosecution filed on 24 March 2005. And it is further subject to the motion for protective measures filed yesterday. I've discussed this with the Defence, and at least counsel for two of the accused indicated they had no problem with that and another was going to get back to me. So I don't know if they have anything to add. But essentially what we're seeking is just that this witness be referred to only by pseudonym and that the materials behind tab 1 be admitted under seal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there any objection? Thank you. The witness list of the Prosecution will be amended to add L97 as a witness. The statement at tab 1 in its redacted form will be admitted by consent under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. And one issue I neglected to mention, last time we marked the index for identification purposes only to help us keep track of the ERN. Perhaps that practice should be followed again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Marked for identification will be the index.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The index, Your Honour, will be P220 MFI. And tab 1 would be P221 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, the materials behind tab 2 are Rule 92 bis materials for Witness L3. This witness was formerly listed as a viva voce witness, but subsequently as part of negotiations with the Defence a new statement was taken and the 92 bis procedure was done, and we have agreed on admission of that evidence in written form. These materials, Your Honour, are subject to both motions filed yesterday, that is the Prosecution's fifth motion for admission pursuant to Rule 92 bis and also the protective measures motion, and I would ask that they receive the next number under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Does your witness list include this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, it does, Your Honour. This witness was previously listed as a viva voce witness, and we would ask that that be changed. And to be clear with regard to protective measures, Your Honour, this witness previously had received protective measures and we would simply seek a variance to permit her to maintain a pseudonym and for her 92 bis materials to be admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And what is her pseudonym?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: L03, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness list of the Prosecution will be amended so that the witness L03 is shown as a Rule 92 bis. The statement at tab 2 will be received as an exhibit pursuant to Rule 92 bis under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number would be P222 for tab 2, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. The materials behind tab 3 are 92 bis materials for Witness L43. Your Honour, this evidence was provisionally admitted by a decision of Your Honours on the 13th of October, 2004, and we have subsequently completed the Rule 92 bis (B) procedure and I would ask that it receive the next exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Was it given an exhibit number when provisionally admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. And I should be clear: What I mean is it was subject to one of the -- I believe this was the Prosecution's first Rule 92 bis motion. At that stage it was provisionally admitted subject to us complying with the attestation requirements of 92 bis (B), which we have now done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Does this need to be under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No, it does not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This statement of Witness L43 will be received pursuant to Rule 92 bis by consent.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 3 will be Prosecution Exhibit P223.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Moving on to tab 4. These are Rule 92 bis materials for Witness L101. These materials are also subject to both of the motions filed by the Prosecution yesterday in which we seek to add the witness to the witness list, we seek the admission of his statement pursuant to Rule 92 bis, and we also seek the protective measures of pseudonym and admission under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The statement at tab 4 will by consent be received pursuant to Rule 92 bis, being the statement of Witness L101. It will be received under seal. Protective measures as moved will be ordered.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 4 will be Prosecution Exhibit P224 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would then move away from the Rule 92 bis witnesses to address the last four items on the index and included in the binder. These are expert materials, all of which have been agreed with the Defence for admission. And again I'll just take them very rapidly one by one. The material behind tab 5 is an expert report bearing the reference number 001/2005ER, dated March 3, 2005. Your Honour, this report from ICMP deals with victims Zvonko Marinkovic, and Jefta Petkovic, and I would ask that it receive the next Prosecution Exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: By consent the expert report of the International Commission on Missing Persons dated 3rd of March, 2005, will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 5 would be Prosecution Exhibit P225.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving on to tab 6. This is another expert report from the International Commission on Missing Persons. The reference number of this report is 003/2004, and it's dated December 12, 2004. Your Honour, this report deals with victim Hasan Hoxha, and I would ask that it receive the next Prosecution Exhibit number. Its admission has been agreed with Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The similar report at tab 6, dated December 12th of December 2004 will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 6 will be Prosecution Exhibit P226.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. The document behind tab 7 is an autopsy report dated 13 October 2003. It bears the case number SLD01/002B, and I would ask that it receive the next exhibit number, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The autopsy report of the 13th of October, 2003, will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be -- tab 7 will be Prosecution Exhibit P227, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The document behind the final tab, tab 8, is a death certificate for Fehmi Xhema, also known as Fehmi Tafa. As you note, it also bears the case number SLD01/002B, and it's signed on the 25th of January, 2005. I would ask that it receive the next exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The death certificate of Fehmi Xhema at tab 8 will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 8 would be Prosecution Exhibit P228, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just by way of forecasting, Your Honour, we do expect another document that will relate to Fehmi Xhema, also known as Fehmi Tafa. We first received word about this identification on the 16th of March, 2005, and since that time I've been working to confirm with ICMP that they have indeed obtained a match for this individual. They confirmed that to me on Friday afternoon, the 8th of April. It does take some time to compile these expert reports and, Your Honour, the Defence have been kind enough to agree that we can admit this report when it comes in. We're working to complete it as soon as we can. I don't know if Your Honour thinks it's appropriate to reserve an exhibit number for it or if we should just deal with the report when it's finalised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think when it comes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure that it was a hundred per Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. cent clear from the record, and that would be my fault if it wasn't clear, but Your Honour was -- specified that the protective measures as requested were granted for Witness L101. Is that also the case for Witnesses L97 and L03 who are also subject to that motion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No. So that will need to be ordered as well. There will be protective measures as moved for Witness L03 and L97.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that all?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm very grateful. That's all I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We're ready for the next witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Would you be kind enough to take the affirmation on the card that is shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I indicate for the benefit of Mr. Black that the decisions in respect of protective measures will be the subject of a written decision. I think as a matter of caution it's always convenient that the precise protective measures ordered be clearly recorded, and they will issue in due course. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Coo.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I know you've testified before, but I forget this myself. Please try to remember: We need to speak a little bit slowly, allow a gap between question and answer to allow for the interpretation to catch up.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Would you please state your full name for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Philip Coo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Most of what we talk about today is going to be the report that you prepared for this case and we'll get to that in a moment, but first could you tell the Court just an outline of your military background before you came to the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I spent ten years as an intelligence officer in the Canadian army. My roles in that -- during that ten years included positions at the National Defence headquarters doing strategic intelligence. I also had an appointment in a division headquarters in an intelligence company, and an appointment at the brigade level including a tour with SFOR in Bosnia in 1996. All of my positions as an intelligence officer involved the conduct of analyses and the supervision of personnel engaged in analyses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving on now, could you tell me, when did you begin your current employment at the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I joined the ICTY in May 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And - excuse me - where do you work within the ICTY? What is your function?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I work in the Office of the Prosecutor in a section called the military analysis team within the investigations division.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what exactly is the military analysis team, or MAT as it's sometimes called?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: The military analysis team is a team of individuals, all of whom have past military experience primarily as intelligence personnel. Their function is to identify and review information pertaining to the armed organisations in the conflicts that we look at in the ICTY and the primary role is analysis of the information that we come across concerning armed groups, the activities of the armed groups, structure of the armed groups, and how those armed groups are commanded and controlled.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And what is your role or title in the MAT?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I'm the head of the military analysis team.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How long have you been the head of the military analysis team?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I became the acting head in August of 2004 and was appointed full-time head in January of 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Since you began working in the military analysis team, have you specialised or focused on any particular area for analysis?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: My focus throughout has been the conflicts pertaining to Kosovo and primarily connected to the Serb accused we have indicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Have you testified previously before the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I did. I testified in the Milosevic case as an expert witness for Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Coo's CV is at tab 2 of the thick binder, differentiated from the last one. I would like to move his CV into evidence. If that could be given a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have drawn this particular straw on behalf of all of us. I indicated in prior conversations with Mr. Nicholls that we have no objection to the CV and indeed to the full report of this witness being placed before you. In fact, we would have been happy for you to have it sometime earlier so you could have read it, digested it and familiarised yourselves with it, but I'm sure we can manage to struggle along with it together today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey, thank you very much for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I thank Attorney Harvey as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The tab 2, the CV of Mr. Coo, will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. And I should say that is U 0083180 through 3184.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P229.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, turning specifically to the report which you prepared in connection with this case, who asked you to prepare it, a report for the Limaj case?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I was asked by Andrew Cayley, the former senior trial attorney for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What is the aim of the report that you wrote?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: The aim of the report is to describe the nature of the armed conflict in Kosovo in 1998 from the months of January through August.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In your report - which, Your Honours, is behind tab 3 - you talk about the scope of the report in paragraphs 1 and 2. Could you just tell us here for the record what the scope of the report was.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: The scope was to describe the reactions of the -- the belligerent forces, the Serb -- the Serb forces and the KLA, their reactions to the deteriorating security situation in Kosovo at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What sources of information did you use in preparing the report?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I relied on information from four general categories. There's information from the Serb FRY and Serb forces, information from the ECMM monitoring mission, the communiques of the KLA, and a variety of miscellaneous reports, which included reports such as the minutes of the joint -- in the FRY joint command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I know this is a rather general question, but can you describe out of those categories which sources you relied on more or which you considered more useful to preparing the report, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: The most useful sources were those in annex B, which come primarily from the Yugoslav army, the VJ. The other primary source was the reports from the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And briefly, we've got your report, but could you tell us what annexes A through E are, what those different annexes represent.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: These were, as I mentioned earlier, the general categories of documentation that I used. Annex A is miscellaneous, and that includes reports that didn't logically fit into the other three categories, and it includes one -- from my recollection, one Serbian press report, the minutes of the joint command, and a small number of other sources. Annex B is primarily the reports from the Yugoslav army and primarily from the Pristina Corps. It also includes some reports from other military structures within Kosovo such as the military territorial organisation represented by the Pristina Military District. Annex C -- I may be mixing up annex B and C, but one of the two is the KLA communiques, and those were a relatively small number of communiques issued through the months that I looked at. And annex D, the ECMM reports were the reports provided to us by the European Commission Monitoring Mission in Kosovo at that time, which had observers on the ground. And annex E was a report produced by the army of Yugoslavia's security administration in Kosovo, and that security administration was a component of the VJ which had, among other things, responsibility for reporting and investigating crimes committed against or by members of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you describe what in your view are the limitations or caveats which should be taken with the report, if any.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: One of them includes the realisation that KLA communiques may have a propaganda element. I took that into account, and I don't believe that that factored into the overall assessment or affected the overall assessment. Other considerations and a fairly significant gap was the absence of reporting from the Ministry of Interior, which is the -- which are the police forces in Kosovo. While we had a lot of documentation from the VJ, documentation on what the Ministry of Interior forces were doing was notably lacking for a variety of reasons, but primarily because responses to requests for assistance weren't met as well as they were by the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to admit the report, please. That's U 0083185 to 3220. And if I can explain. The report itself and the citations and supporting material comprise five to seven large binders, so what we've done is one set in hard copy which will go in as an exhibit, and we've provided three copies on CD for Your Honours. The CD -- four. I'm sorry. Four CDs. The CD contains the entire report with all of the footnotes and annexes hyperlinked. In other words, one can click on the ERN number and then read the document that is in the footnote. I think that works better and should work on everybody's system. If at any point Your Honours do not like using that CD method, we will substitute hard copies, and counsel have agreed to that very generously.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we could give that a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The report at tab 3 of the witness will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think, Your Honours, if we give --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The question being asked of me is what about all the attachments?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's why if we give the number to the CD and one Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. number to the hard copy, that includes the report and all of the attachments and supporting material. I think that can be given one number. It may be the best way to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you want two separate numbers?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. One number, I think, for the report and all of the attachments which would be in CD, but just in case, if we could have the same number on the hard copy or a /1 or something of that nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I was misled by you giving page numbers at the beginning when you moved. Very well. We will receive the complete report, both so far as we have it in hard copy and in CD form, as one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P230.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Coo -- oh, I'm sorry, one last point: Mr. Coo, is it correct that you found a couple mistakes, I think dates, in translation that you corrected?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I provided an erratum.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is a very short errata sheet that was given to the Defence yesterday. If this could be given an exhibit number. It should be a different number because it's not actually part of the CD or the body of the report and the materials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The errata report will be received as a separate exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P231.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Coo, in paragraphs 44 to 48 of your report, the very end of your report, you give an assessment of the nature of the armed conflict in Kosovo between January and September 1998, and we'll go through a lot of the documents which led you to that assessment, but maybe if we could start with you giving the Court just a shorthand explanation of your assessment of the nature of the conflict during that period.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. During the period January to approximately mid-May 1998, the information that I had suggested that the conflict between the Serb forces and the KLA was comprised of relatively sporadic incidents increasing through -- through to mid-May. And then again on the basis of the information reviewed, sometime in mid-May things seemed to have picked up in intensity and geographical spread and operations were occurring on a much more widespread basis, and this continued through -- with increasing intensity again through July and at least into early August 1998. In July 1998, the -- June 1998 and through July, the Serb forces launched a large offensive in Kosovo. Prior to that, the offensives were fairly intense, but in particular it was July when the -- the offensive picked up and involved the whole of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll now move into the body of the report from the beginning. You start off explaining in paragraphs 4 to 8 the structure of the VJ, and we have a map in paragraph 7 which shows the AORs, or areas of responsibility, of the different units. What was the name of the corps which had responsibility for Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: The Pristina Corps had the area of responsibility covering Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what military body was above the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Its superior formation was the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And in paragraph 5 and 6 you talk about the units which comprised the Pristina Corps. You can look at your report if you need to, I think, because there's a lot of them. It's at tab 3. You state that these units were subordinate during peacetime. Can you just explain what you mean by that. Which units were active at all times and which would be activated in a time of conflict?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: The Pristina Corps had a number of subordinate brigades, some of which were active even in peacetime, others would only be activated during a state of emergency or other extraordinary state such as a state of war, and during peacetime these inactive units were kept at cadre strength with a small core personnel. The active brigades included the 15th Armoured Brigade, the 125th Motorised Brigade, the 243rd Mechanised Brigade, the 549th Motorised Brigade, and there were also two artillery brigades, the 52nd Mixed Artillery Brigade and the 52nd Air Defence and Rocket Artillery Brigade. The first four units I listed are what is -- are what are known as manoeuvre units and they perform a combat function. The other two units, the artillery units support these by providing artillery support. Additional units included the military police and reconnaissance units. And military police in the Yugoslav army had a combat function, whereas in some armies military police don't have that function. In the Yugoslav army they had a -- they conducted special operations and would be used in particular against insurgent forces or for special targets. When I mentioned the peacetime structure of the brigade, that's a reference to the fact that during wartime the brigade could be reinforced. It would be brought up to strength by having its inactive units manned, but it could also be reinforced by units from outside the -- from outside the corps. And this happened in 1999 when a number of brigades were brought in from outside. But it also happened during the period reviewed for this report. There are at least two brigades, or elements of two brigades that were brought in from outside, outside Kosovo, and those were the 72nd Special Forces Brigade and the 63rd Parachute Brigade. They normally belonged to the Special Forces Corps based in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. If Mr. Younis could put on Sanction the map which appears in paragraph 7 of the report. It's not working on Sanction. If we could have it on the ELMO. Your Honours, this is simply a colour copy of the map in paragraph 7 I would like to admit because it does not come through clearly either on the CD or in the printed report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for clarity, I should add that you can note that it's the 52nd Corps on that map. The 52nd Corps is another name for the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you can see that on your monitor, Mr. Coo, that is the same map showing the areas of responsibilities of the different brigades that's in your report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we could give that a number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P232.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Coo. The next area I want to briefly discuss, which is found in paragraphs 9 to 14 of your report, is the structure of the Serbian Ministry of Internal Affairs, or the MUP. In 1998, you talk about this in your report, under the law of the FRY was there any role for the MUP in armed combat?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: The FRY law on defence recognises that the MUP has a combat function and takes that into account by stating that during extraordinary states such as a state of war the MUP can be used in combat operations, and when this occurs, that they should be subordinated to the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And in 1998, was any such state of emergency declared, or war?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: To my knowledge there was no such emergency in 1998. Despite that, the MUP did conduct combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 11 of your report you talk about MUP units which were specially trained and equipped for combat; the PJP, the SAJ, and the JSO. Could you please explain to us what those different units were, what they were intended for.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: All of those units are MUP special units. They're all very heavily armed and they have special training for the conduct of combat operations. The largest of them is the PJP, or special police units. They're drawn from the regular police and members of the regular police are given special training, and they're called up when required during emergencies. They were called up almost full-time in Kosovo during this part of 1998 and in 1999. They -- their structure is very much like a light infantry unit in the military. They have mortars, armoured personnel carriers. They use air defence artillery systems against ground targets, and a variety of other heavy weapons. Two more special units, and much smaller units, are the JSO, the Special Operations Unit, and the SAJ, which is a Special Anti-Terrorist Unit. They have much -- much -- a much higher standard of training. They're quite a bit smaller. Their total size at that time was estimated at about 500 for each unit, and their roles was to conduct operations such as the attacks against KLA headquarters, and their particular speciality would be to -- or ability would be to infiltrate deep into territory held by the KLA. And I should add that the PJP structure -- the PJP was structured along military lines with companies and detachments, and each company would have 120 to 150 personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. In paragraph 14, you talk about an entity called the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija. Can you tell me what that organisation was and what its -- the function of the MUP staff was in 1998.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: The MUP staff had existed since at least the beginning of 1998. Its function was to coordinate the activities of the Ministry of the Interior units in Kosovo. Typically in Serbia. This was the Serbian MUP. There was a federal MUP which was of no relevance at this time, but the Serbian MUP was structured into a regional system of secretariats. Kosovo had seven secretariats. Typically, each secretariat would report to the ministry headquarters in Belgrade. In Kosovo, the situation was sufficiently serious that they set up a MUP staff, a headquarters within Kosovo to coordinate the functions of the seven secretariats. So rather than gaining the direction directly from Belgrade, the secretariats were being coordinated by the MUP staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we look, please, at the document behind tab 5, and that should be in your binder as well, Mr. Coo. This is ERN 03008251 for the first page. And for the record, this is from footnote 20 of the report. It's the decision on the formation of the staff of the ministry in Pristina. And we can see on the second page that it's dated 15th of May, 1998. Could you just tell us quickly, Mr. Coo, what -- what the significance of this document is.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: This is a reiteration of the existence of the MUP staff, and it reflects newly appointed members of the MUP staff which isn't shown in here at the time, but in May 1998 General Sreten Lukic was appointed head of the MUP staff, and at that time it was a formality to reissue the mandate of the MUP staff, and that's what this document is. And it shows that their role, their function was to coordinate activities of the MUP in Kosovo, and these activities included suppression of civil disorder, terrorism, and rebellion, as paragraph 2(a) shows. This document is signed by an assistant minister in the ministry who was head of the public security department. There were two departments in the ministry. One was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the public security department, the other the state security department. So at this time, the function of the MUP staff was -- or the mandate of the MUP staff pertained to -- solely to the units of the public security department in Kosovo, and public security included the PJP and regular police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we could quickly look at the previous document at tab 4, 03077941, which is from footnote 19. The decision to establish a ministerial staff for the suppression of terrorism, this time dated 16th of June. It's a bit confusing, both of these documents a month apart talking about a similar topic. Could you explain what this document tells us in relation to the one we just looked at.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document expands the role of the MUP staff by incorporating the state security division of the MUP. And because of that, because it covers the whole of the MUP, it's signed off by the minister, Vlajko Stojiljkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So then if I understand at this point, all MUP units are being coordinated by this body.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's correct. And for example, the assistant head for special operations, Milorad Lukovic was the head of the JSO, which is a state security special unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: From January to August, who was in overall command of the MUP in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Sreten Lukic was in overall command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I should have asked you this earlier, but who was in command of the PRK or Pristina Corps during this time?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: General Nebojsa Pavkovic was commanding the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What about the chains of commands for these two, for the MUP and for the Pristina Corps? Were they separate or in the same chain during the period of your report?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Each had their own chain of command. The MUP reported -- the MUP units reported up through their secretariats and/or through the MUP staff, and from the MUP staff up to Belgrade, to the ministry. The Pristina Corps had its chain of command whereby the field units reported through the brigades, brigades to the corps, corps to the army, and the army to the General Staff in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to move on now, going through your report chronologically. The next sort of armed force you talk about or grouping or local defence unit, that's in paragraph 15 to 21 of the report, what were local defence units?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: The local defence is an unofficial term to cover a collective of various organisations which were formed to -- put together to defend villages and small towns in Kosovo. The composition of these village defence forces or town defence forces included civilian -- the civilian defence organisation which was a Federal Ministry of Defence organisation. It included the MUP represented by MUP reservists. It also included the military territorial organisation which was represented in Kosovo by the Pristina Military District, and that was an organisation that formed small units, and its primary purpose was administering conscription for -- on behalf of the VJ. But it also had a secondary role of forming armed units. Also in local defence were armed civilians, and there was an official process by which civilians in Kosovo of Serb and Montenegrin descent were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In connection with that could we look at the document at tab 6. 03036751 is the ERN number. It's footnote 21 in your report. This is a 21st of May, 1998 document. It's an order on the implementation of measures for security and protection of the population. Could you please explain to us why you included this in your report and cited it.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Just for clarification, Your Honours, I think it's footnote -- or tab 6, not tab 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Tab 6. That's right. It's footnote 21. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: This comes from the head of the civilian defence organisation in Kosovo. Civilian defence was the federal structure that was responsible for civilian defence, the mandate of which was to form armed guards to protect vital installations during times of crisis, to perform other functions such as rescuing the population, clearing rubble, and a variety of other tasks. In this document the head of the civilian defence unit is reacting to a situation by which it was noted that Serb -- ethnic Serbs were arming themselves because of the deteriorating situation in Kosovo, and the government had obviously decided to address this by formalising and making official the creation of local defence units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I think that's reflected in the first full paragraph, the explanation for why this order is being given; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to ask you now about a topic you address, an institution you address in paragraph 17, the Joint Command for Kosovo. What was that institution?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: The Joint Command was formed in June 1998 by President Milosevic. Its function was to -- involved sending down representatives from his government and representatives of the government in Kosovo to enable political oversight of the activities in Kosovo at that time and to ensure that the -- the aims of the government in Belgrade were realised and coordinated in Kosovo so that all the institutions in Kosovo dealing with the problem; the political institutions, the civil affairs institutions, and the armed organisations, the MUP and the VJ, all acted in a coordinated fashion. So they established this body called the Joint Command which met on a regular basis and discussed events and decided on how future events would be conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And can you tell us, was this a unique institution or one that had existed before in the FRY? Can you just talk about that a little bit.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such organisation existing before, nor could I find any reference to such an organisation existing in the doctrine or the laws or constitution of the FRY or Serbia. It's not uncommon. It was -- a similar organisation was established in 2001 when they had a problem with ethnic Albanians in South Serbia in the Presevo area. It makes sense to have political oversight on scene in a crisis area, but I haven't seen any examples of such a situation -- such a structure in Kosovo prior to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 19 of your report you talk about the role of the MUP in local defence and a document which is at tab 7, "The joint command's instructions for the defence of inhabited places." This is 03037896. It's from footnote 23. Can you just tell us about the significance of these instructions which were issued in July.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: These instructions, Your Honour, seemed to recognise the seriousness of the problem in Kosovo, that it was sufficiently serious at that time to set up fairly capable local defence units. The -- the instruction makes it apparent that the local defence wasn't just going to consist of handing locals a hunting rifle or a pistol. It included references to the use of artillery and to the conduct of combat operations including offensive combat operations rather than purely defensive operations. It also incorporated the -- considered incorporation of the army of Yugoslavia, the MUP, and other armed organisations in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if we look at section 2 of this document, which is on page 3, "Forces for the defence of towns and their purpose," the instructions speak of the role of the MUP, to organise, lead, and perform combat operations and the support of VJ units through artillery. Can you tell us whether -- whether that occurred, as far as your other research and documentation has shown?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I don't know if it occurred exactly as set out in this paragraph in relation to defence of a village, but I do know that from the documentation, much of which is included in the report, and especially in annex B, that the MUP and the VJ did conduct joint operations, and their standard tactic was that the MUP performed the function of an infantry unit where they would conduct the attack on the target which sometimes would include a village, and the VJ would provide support through heavy weapons such as artillery, mortars, and tank fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we look at page 7 of this document, section 5, Commanding, under the instructions, who was to primarily command these village or town defence units?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: According to this instruction, the commands of local defence units was held by a MUP officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I don't want to go through them all because it's a large document, but you included the minutes of the Joint Command, the body which issued these instructions in Annex A of your report. For the record, that's at tab 27, the ERN is 03085476. But without going through all of those minutes, why did you include them in your report and what can be learned from reading these minutes?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: The minutes show the meetings of the Joint Command occurring on a -- an almost daily basis. The subjects they cover included the occurrences in the -- in Kosovo during the day, with plenty of references to armed confrontations. In addition, the minutes make reference to what the VJ and the MUP in particular are expected to undertake in the subsequent days. The minutes also show who is in the joint command and playing what role. And, for example, it shows that at least at every meeting there was a representative, a senior representative from the MUP, the VJ, and the civilian administration in Kosovo as well as the representatives from Belgrade, Milomir Minic and Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you remember, when did these meetings start taking place with the representatives you've just told us about?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: The minutes -- I think the first day of the minutes is the 22nd, or it might be the 27th of July, 1998. The Joint Command was created in June 1998. What I should -- I should add that from the minutes it's clear that the Joint Command is performing a coordination role. It's coordinating the activities of the VJ and the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm about to start a new topic, Your Honour. Maybe, if Your Honours wish, we could break now, rather than just get three minutes into it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you for that indication. It will be necessary for the Chamber to take a half-hour break at this time, so we will resume at a quarter past four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Coo, I now want to turn to the real meat of the report, paragraphs 22 to 43, which you've entitled "The nature of the conflict." There's been quite a lot of testimony already in this case about the Serb forces attack in March on Prekaz in the Drenica region. Can you briefly tell us the significance of those attacks in terms of the impact on the military situation and on combat. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Based on the information I reviewed, that attack in particular seems to have galvanised the Kosovo Albanian community, and in response the KLA seems to have increased -- seemed to have increased the intensity of its operations in Kosovo, and that's reflected in the documentation. The operations became much more intensive in mid-May and July, but there was certainly a change after the incident at Prekaz.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to now look at the views expressed by some senior VJ commanders at the time in July 1998. If we turn to tab 8, which is 03039554 and is footnote 34 to your report, on page 57 of that document you've cited and talked quite extensively about a letter from General Pavkovic of 23 July, 1998 to the collegium, the 3rd Army command. First of all, what period of time is General Pavkovic talking about in his letter to the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Your Honours, from the first paragraph it seems that General Pavkovic is reflecting the situation from the previous two months, so presumably through June and -- through at least mid-May through June and until the letter was written in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if we look at paragraphs 2 and 3, what are the problems that General Pavkovic is identifying or what is the purpose of this letter to his superiors?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: The implication in paragraph 2, and it's supported by other documents, but the implication solely from paragraph 2 is that Serb forces have been conducting operations or have been engaged in confrontations in Kosovo during the period that General Pavkovic is referring to. He cites problems with the MUP's ability to deal with the problem effectively, and the MUP certainly isn't as well trained in combat as the VJ, so the implication is and the statement that General Pavkovic seems to be making is that more needs to be done than has been done up to that point and the VJ should be involved in a much more extensive way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And can you comment generally on this document, what it means to see this type of letter using this type of language describing events, "the situation increasing at dizzying speed," if that has any meaning to you in your analysis.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: It's typically unusual for a subordinate commander to address his superior commander in a manner that strong. The wording of the document is quite strong. The situation as described by Pavkovic seems to have become fairly dire, and Pavkovic has, I would presume up until that point, had tried every possible -- every reasonable means to get the superior command and the VJ and the state to recognise that the VJ had to be involved in a more extensive manner if the situation was to be dealt with effectively. He must have been feeling fairly frustrated by this point and driven to write such a strongly worded document to his superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I rise with some trepidation having said that I'm perfectly happy for the witness's reporting to go in full, but when we get into speculating as to what was in the mind and what were the feelings of a general who as far as I know this witness has never met still has discussed those feelings I think we're going a little bit far, with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps the document and its contents should be allowed to speak for itself, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think that's fine, Your Honour. I would just say that as an expert with his background in intelligence he's reviewed thousands of military documents. He may be able to make some valid assessments based on the extraordinary nature, but I think the document does speak for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And again, you started talking about this, and I think you've answered it, but what solution is he proposing for the problem in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: General Pavkovic is proposing more extensive use of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we go to tab 9, this is 03055097, footnote 35 to your report. On page 3 of that document we have a letter also 23 July 1998, from General Momcilo Perisic, and can you tell us who General Perisic was?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: General Perisic at that time was the chief of the General Staff of the VJ, which meant that he was the commander of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And he is sending this letter to President Milosevic. Can you tell us the significance of this letter of the same date, why you included it in your report, what it means to you.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I included this -- this letter from General Perisic for a number of reasons, one of which was General Perisic remarks that in April 1998, he had asked for the creation of a declaration of a state of emergency in Kosovo, and the description of a state of emergency in FRY law suggests that a state of emergency, and by its name alone suggests that a state of emergency would be declared when the situation becomes critical. So in April 1998, the Chief of the General Staff of the VJ felt that the security situation in Kosovo was sufficiently drastic that it warranted the declaration of a state of emergency.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if you look on page 4, can you discuss General Perisic's proposed solution? It begins about the middle of the page to "use the VJ lawfully to defend the border areas ..." and so on.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: During peacetime, one of the VJ's roles is defence of the border areas, defence of the border areas of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and this is a role that in the absence of a state of emergency General Perisic felt the VJ should be dedicated to in Kosovo, and he suggests that the VJ had, at the time of the writing of the letter, been engaged in other tasks, and the other documents that I refer to in the report support this allegation by General Perisic. So General Perisic is proposing that the VJ be engaged in a more extensive fashion in Kosovo but in accordance with the constitution and the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you look at also on page 4 3(b), which is attempts by unauthorised persons to command VJ units and his proposals to solve that problem, could you just discuss the significance of that section of his letter.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Again there's the implication in there that the VJ has been used in combat operations up until that point, but Perisic -- General Perisic disagreed with the way, the manner in which it was tasked, and he thought that the Joint Command was acting outside the legal provisions for commanding the VJ. He describes the way in which the Joint Command was set up to work and claims that it's acting in violation of that, and he's proposing that the VJ be commanded in its proper legal fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: One of the things he proposes is that the 3rd Army set up a forward command post in the Pristina sector. Just tell us, what is a forward command post?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: When operations are ongoing, it's quite common for a military headquarters to establish a forward command post, which -- which fulfils a command function, a headquarters function, but what it does is it puts the commander closer to the scene of action, so closer to the front lines. The purpose of that is so that the commander can gain better insight into the situation. For instance, it -- it means that it's much easier for him to visit units that are engaged in combat operations. It's -- information gets to the commander much more quickly and he can respond to it in a much more timely fashion. So in this instance, General Perisic's proposition that a forward command post for not just the Pristina Corps be formed but the 3rd Army headquarters and the 3rd Army headquarters is outside Kosovo, so that his proposition that they bring an element of the 3rd Army command into Kosovo to oversee what was going on there also suggests that the situation in Kosovo at that time was sufficiently serious to warrant such an act.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Was a forward command post of the 3rd Army set up in Kosovo in 1998?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: It was in July 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What about for the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: The Pristina Corps had a forward command post from at least, I think, about the 21st of April. Certainly in April 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that's for the same reasons which you've just explained as for the 3rd Army forward command post?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to now focus on the months May, June, and July, and documents which illustrate combat operations during those months in Kosovo. If we look first at tab 10. This is 03060812, footnote 31 to your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document has previously been exhibited in the testimony of Mr. Crosland and was given the exhibit number P092 T17, so you have seen this document before. It's a 13th of May, 1998 urgent document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to go through this document, Mr. Coo, in a little more detail than we will the rest. First of all, can you just tell us what this document is, what the function of this document is.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the commander of the Pristina Corps, General Pavkovic, writing to his superior command, the 3rd Army, in response to what looks like an estimate produced by the 3rd Army on the previous day for -- for how the Pristina Corps could be deployed to react to the situation in Kosovo, and General Pavkovic is responding with a description of how the corps has deployed up until that point and propositions for further deployments and further responses to the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how does he -- and he starts talking about this in paragraph 1. How does he characterise the situation he's facing in May, mid-May 1998?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: The characterisation is one of a deteriorating security situation and resulting -- arising from the increasing number of KLA attacks, and he identifies what he -- or what his staff, his intelligence staff, has identified as the likely intentions or aims of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And he places KLA forces at this time at between 3.500 and 4.500 men?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you look on page 2 of the document, the second paragraph, can you comment on his estimates of the territory held by the KLA at that time?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: General Pavkovic has commented that about 30 per cent of the territory of Kosovo and Metohija is being put under the control of the KLA. And he also further defines that by identifying the key lines of communication or the key roads in Kosovo that are under their control. This estimate, and it would come from his intelligence staff based on reports that are coming into the Pristina Corps, is corroborated by, for example, ECMM reports at around the same time where they claim that the KLA seemed to control roughly that amount of territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if you look down under 2.1, we see: "In the period between 21 April and 12 May 1998 the following forces were engaged in the corps' zone of responsibility ..." Just to be clear, he's talking about what forces under his command have been engaged in the prior period?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's correct. And he identifies the roles that they've been given.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And there's the acronym BG-1 and BG-2. What do those stand for?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Those are B/C/S acronyms for the English term "combat group," and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. a combat group in this context is a military unit formed on a temporary basis to conduct specific combat operations. It's formed -- combat groups are formed from the battalions within a particular brigade and they are company plus in size, which means that they're over 150 personnel. They usually include infantry, armour, and artillery. The fact that you would form combat groups suggests that they have in mind the requirement to conduct combat operations or they were conducting combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then just generally, without going through it line by line, can you tell us your assessment of what he is proposing for the deployment of his forces in the coming months, because he's broken up the document of what is to be accomplished by 1st of June, by the 15th of June, and so on.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: He's -- in general terms he's proposing the broader engagement of the Pristina Corps units, and he identifies some of the tasks that he envisions them undertaking, such as clearing the lines of communication, which are primarily those three roads cutting across Kosovo that he identified as being held by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could jump ahead now to tab 13. This has been previously exhibited, Your Honours, as P048. It's the KLA communique number 47, U 0038573. Unfortunately, on this copy, because of the highlighting that came through, it's difficult to see it's communique 47. You can see it more clearly on the screen in Sanction. Now, this KLA communique is coming out on the -- it's issued on the 12th of May, right about the same time as the proposal we just saw from Pavkovic. Can you comment on this KLA communique and what it claims about the control of territory and control of roads.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: In general terms, the description provided in the communique corroborates what was in the 13th of May report from the Pristina Corps, which describes the KLA holding 30 per cent of the territory, conducting operations over a wide area in Kosovo, and here in the communique the KLA is claiming that they are conducting such operations. The geographical spread of those operations corresponds roughly to what was described in the 13th of May report from the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if we look towards the bottom of the communique, it states: "In lightning action by military formations an operation against the enemy's punitive expeditions on the main road in the operational subzone of Pastrik was successfully carried out."

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Again that shows the VJ's intent and involvement in regaining control of the lines of communication appears to be going on and it corroborates what the KLA is saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could look at tab 14, R025-2507. This is an ECMM report from the 15th of May, 1998. So the same time frame, given one or two days. You included this in your report. If we look at the second page, last paragraph, it states: "MT" -- and before I continue, can you just tell us what MT stands for?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's mobile team.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "Mobile team Belgrade's observations on the ground hint that another crucial corner has been turned in Kosovo. The UCK until a few weeks ago still a mystery with its structure, leadership, tactics and funding sources and political connections widely unknown, has come to life and into focus of public attention. From a more defensive posture during the February and March clashes, the UCK has now taken the initiative and is carrying the 'war' to the Serbian security forces. An example of the change in their tactics has been the closure of the Pristina-Pec road, the main supply route for the Serbian security forces, for more than four days." I think that's pretty clear but could you comment on what ECM is reporting in relation to the Pavkovic report and the KLA communique.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Again, this is further corroboration for the assessment that the intensity of operations picked up around mid-May, and -- and that the KLA was at least by then having some success in coordinating its operations centrally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Still in May. I'm sorry to jump around. If we could go back to tab 11. That's ET 80227948, also from, I should say, annex B to your report. This is the 28th of May, 1998, "very urgent decision on engagement." Could you just tell us what this document is about and why you included it in your report.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: This document shows or assists with the description of the armed conflict in Kosovo. It shows that combat operations were being conducted by -- by the VJ, and they -- these combat operations included the use of heavy weapons such as tanks, suggesting that the threat must have been fairly serious to require the use of tanks and artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if we look at paragraph 2, the tanks and artillery are to be used for the purpose of supporting MUP forces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's correct. Again, it shows that the MUP were involved in the combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the next tab, number 12, please ET K0227950. This appears in footnote 47 of your report. This is the 29th of May 1998 order for the Pristina Corps units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document on the CD and in the hard copies had a couple of important translation errors. I'm behind Mr. Younis. He's fixed it in the hard copy. Sorry, Your Honours. It has been corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In the CD as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm told that it has been.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, what is this? This is an order, very urgent, number 1, to "raise to full combat readiness the permanent composition of the Pristina Corps by 1200 hours on 29 May 1998." Can you just tell us what the implications are of this kind of order putting the entire Pristina Corps on full combat readiness.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Your Honours, putting the full corps on combat readiness essentially makes the units of the corps have to be put into a position where they are prepared to deploy and conduct combat operations on very short notice, in a matter of hours. To do this suggests that again the situation was sufficiently tense and drastic to take this measure. The placing of a military unit on full combat readiness is a fairly serious step to take because it doesn't take very long before the unit becomes tired. It eats up a lot of resources. It involves the cancellation of leave and the unit's personnel either have to be in barracks all the time or in the field in specified locations all the time and ready to come to the unit within a matter of minutes. So prior to this, units of the Pristina Corps had been involved in combat already, but now by the end of May they've seen the necessity of putting the full corps on combat readiness, or at least the active units of the corps, which is five, six brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how many, just for those who haven't been in the military, how many men, how many troops is that, five or six brigades?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: The active strength of the corps at this time was about 10.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. You obviously cite and have in annex B many more documents, also in your other annexes about May, but that's all I want to go through in court to highlight May. If we could go to tab 16, please. This is ET K022-7985, dated 16th of June, 1998, a Pristina Corps forward combat post report. Could you tell us why this report's significant in terms of its explanation of the use of combat groups and the other information in the document.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
