utterances.text: This is a report from the Pristina Corps forward command post, and it describes in -- on the second page in paragraph 2 incidents involving units of the VJ combat -- describing combat activity. So the report was included because it's a -- it provides a description of combat activity at this time in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The report also states in 2.2 that there were no -- it called them terrorist activities against the MUP, and no attacks were registered during this day. Why are attacks against the MUP contained in VJ reports?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: It's crucial that the commander who is deploying forces has all relevant information at hand, and because the MUP and the VJ were conducting combat operations together, or even if they were conducting them separately it required coordination, and it was important to know what was happening to the MUP. And additionally, it also provides some sense of the scale of the activity of the KLA at the time by reporting on -- on what attacks the KLA's conducting, whether it's against the VJ or against non-VJ personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you look at section 5, which is on page 3 of the document, it talks about the decision has been made to continue with increased security of the DG, which is the acronym for the state border, with Albania and prevent entry of DTS, which I think has been stated earlier as terrorist or sabotage groups bringing weapons and ammunition into the territory. Can you just discuss a little bit what the mandate of the VJ was at this time in terms of the state border, the borders of Kosovo as well as the interior.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Aside from the crossing points themselves on the state border, which was a MUP and a customs responsibility, the actual length of the border was the responsibility of the VJ, the patrolling and manning of border posts along the border. And there was a border zone which changed in depth in 1998 and 1999 to allow the VJ more manoeuvre room, but the purpose of defending the border at this time was that the VJ was responsible for countering the flow of KLA and weapons for the KLA coming in from -- primarily from Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Go to tab 17, please. L0044196. This is a 16th of June, 1998, regular operative report to the 3rd Army, talking about an attack on the police station in Rudnik, Srbica. Can you just talk a little bit about this report and the attack which it describes.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: This report is from the organisation I described earlier, which is the military territorial organisation, which also had formed combat units at this time, and the military territorial district in Kosovo was subordinate to the 3rd Army. So here it's reporting on -- on its activities to the 3rd Army. And its description of the attack on the police station suggests that of the -- at least in this incident the KLA was capable of fairly sustained operations, it wasn't just conducting hit-and-run type operations. Additionally, there's a description of the weapons that the KLA were using, which included rocket launchers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can look now at tab 18. It's ET K022-7991. The next day, another report. Can you describe the situation described in this report, what's going on in mid-June.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: This describes an attempt by a group of KLA to cross from Albania into Kosovo, and they were intercepted by a VJ unit and some of the KLA killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Go to tab 19, please. This is the next day now, the 18th of June, 1998, L0053341. Another document from the military district command, and it's discussing the abduction that day of several persons and talking about a previous abduction, persons from the Spasic family. Why -- why would abductions of this nature, why are they contained Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in an operative report to the 3rd Army command?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Your Honours, again this is an example of a requirement that a military command has as much relevant information at hand as possible and such information would be taken from his intelligence staff and used to formulate assessments about the likely intentions of the KLA, that -- to understand the tactics of the KLA, to attempt to understand where they may attack next, their size and a variety of other things that assist a commander in deploying his forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you look at tab 20 now, please, 03035353, the 20th of June, another report to the 3rd Army command, again talking about the abductions of Serbs, the expulsions of families, and the KLA fortifying positions along the Peja-Pristina road in Klina municipality. Could you just comment on -- I think it's the same as the last report, but why this report is significant, why you include it in your report.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: This also describes on one day in 1998, in June, why -- what the KLA were doing, and in this instance of note is that they're fortifying their positions along one of the key lines of communication, the Pec-Pristina road. It also is one of a number of references that I came across to kidnappings, and it seems that it's possible based on that information that that was one of the tactics that the KLA decided would suit their aims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Those are some of the VJ documentations from June. I'd like to now look at a few, not all of them, but some of the ECMM reports included for June in your report, and the first one is at tab 22, R025-4317. That's an ECMM report from the 9th of June, 1998. The first heading under General, the first statement is that: "The so-called liberated area is growing." And then there's a discussion of the security situation. Could you just comment on -- on this report, this ECMM report which you've included.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: This ECMM report is roughly the same time frame as the VJ assessment of the situation, the extent to which the KLA controlled Kosovo and the KLA's communique from mid-May describing where they were conducting operations and the lines of control that they -- communication that they controlled. This ECMM report corroborates those sources of information and corroborates the assessment or supports the assessment that the intensity of operations was picking up at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In the first paragraph of your report states, speaking of the KLA: "As usual they were armed with AK-47, rifles, and RPG 7." What's an RPG?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's a rocket propelled grenade. It's an anti-armour weapon, or it can be used against bunkers as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if you continued down in that same security paragraph, the report talks about the enlargement of the so-called liberated area, the road from Suva Reka to Orahovac no longer being under the control of the Serb forces. And then it describes the -- what they've seen in Djakovica: "Almost all the houses bear evidence of heavy fighting: All glass is broken, bullet impacts of several calibres, mortar impacts on roofs, arson ruins, numerous houses are completely destroyed." Can you just - again it's fairly clear - but comment on what the report is saying there.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: It again suggests that the KLA is having some successes in expanding the area of control and it's further support for the assessment that there were fairly extensive combat operations going on in Kosovo at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we look at tab 3 [sic] Now; R025-4308, another ECMM report, this one from the 16th of June, 1998. Tab 23. It says 3 on the transcript. Under "General," item 2, we see: "The TM are now encountering more KLA checkpoints than Serb, who have abandoned many of their former positions and significant swathes of territory appear now to be in KLA control with the central action of the main Pec-Pristina road from an area east of Kijevo in KLA control thus connecting KLA to the south at Malisevo with those to the north in Drenica." Can you just tell us what this means.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Again it's the expansion of the KLA's area of control, and in order to -- to expand in that fashion, it's -- it's assessed and supported by other documents that there was combat operations involved in the gaining of that territory. I should probably add that when I looked at ECMM reports, I tended to ignore the references and the citations of media reports that they include in many of their daily reports. I only tended to use the parts that were clearly the direct observations of their monitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Again if we look down at paragraph 6, they've talked about Mailsevo above but the report states that: "Malisevo is central to the so-called 'liberated territory' and our efforts to gain the swiftest exit from the area was not possible due to KLA/Serb forces activity along the periphery of this territory in areas close to Suhareke and Orahovac." It's simply another indication of the conflict, the combat in that area in June?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we can look at tab 24, please, R025-4306, another ECMM report from the 17th of June, 1998. Could you just look at 2(a) and (b) and comment on those sections.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: This is describing activities in central Drenica area and it corroborates VJ reporting that the VJ is operating with the MUP, conducting combat operations, and it also corroborates the existence of local defence units in some capacity where they describe Serb civilians manning checkpoints, armed Serb civilians manning checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And at tab 25, R025-4294, 22nd of June, 1998. This is an assessment of the KLA by the ECMM. Could you just discuss the significance of this document where the ECMM is now discussing KLA territory and KLA control of the roads.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: The ECMM at this time is confirming that based on the information available to them, much of which would come from their observers, the KLA's control of the territory was quite extensive and that the -- the KLA was taking on the appearance or had taken on the appearance of a larger organisation at that point, which included very simple village -- villagers acting in a local capacity with fairly basic weapons to a more full-time, professional cadre of KLA members. That is described under the "UCK membership" paragraph. I should probably add that based on this reporting that the KLA's covered such a wide area and managed to gain control of such a wide area in the seemingly relatively short time is suggestive of some -- some ability on the KLA's part to centrally control what its units were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you look under the section "Road infrastructure," the ECMM reports states: "The most striking aspect to much of the KLA-held territory described, is the extent to which the KLA have utilised and improved the local infrastructure, with small roads now being used to ensure a wholly integrated territory that can aid swift movement between areas. In essence, it appears that much thought and probably more strategy has gone into the taking of this territory than most observers felt was likely."

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: The ECMM seemed at this point a bit surprised by how well organised the KLA appears to be. The ability to -- to seize control of territory and retain control of territory of such a wide geographic area suggests that it is a lot more than just villagers taking up arms and acting locally. It would require some successful coordination between various KLA units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And looking at the documents we've just been going through, if you think back to the 13th of May Pristina Corps submission by General Pavkovic, can you comment on -- on his predictions of the way the situation appeared to be developing in May to him now that we've looked at documents from May and June?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: His predictions that the situation would intensify and the KLA increase in strength seem accurate, seem to be accurately reflected in the observations of the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could go to tab 26 now. This is the last ECMM document I'm going to look at for June. This is R025-4282, 29th of June, 1998. There is in the beginning, under the "General" heading, a reference to "significant Serb police action launched at the KLA-held mining village of --" if I pronounce it correctly -- "Belacevac," and then further discussion of KLA control of the roads. Then it talks about the team, with the assistance of Serb police, met coach passengers who had recently been stopped by the KLA at Crnoljevo itself and had four Serb passengers taken hostage. If we turn the page to "Humanitarian affairs," section 3, we see the report: "On reaching the Serb police checkpoint west of Stimlje, local Serb police asked to speak to passengers from a coach which had just been stopped by KLA --" I'm having difficulty with pronunciation today -- "at Crnoljevo village and had four Serb male passengers seized. Of the four men, one was said to be an officer of the VJ, another unknown, and two more a father and son. The wife of the last two was distraught and close to hysteria, but the police were able to explain that they were Serb refugees from the Krajina who were travelling to Pristina in order for UNHCR to process their application for emigration." And then under "Comment: ICRC and the UN High Commission for Human Rights representative in Pristina are increasingly concerned with this recent KLA strategy, with well over 30 Serbs now taken hostage. ICRC have had no access to those taken and have been frustrated in their attempts to find a relevant competent Albanian authority with whom they can discuss the issue." That's fairly self-explanatory as well, but it connects, does it not, to your earlier comment about kidnapping being reported in VJ documents as something of importance and an indication of new tactics?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So the last document for June, Your Honours, a new document, it's a last document in the bundle, tab 47, a New York Times article from 30th of June, 1998, U 0088012. You didn't use this in the report and you didn't use any news reports, did you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: As far as I recall I used one news report, a Tanjug report from earlier in the conflict, but that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you've had a chance to look at this article talking -- which talks about the June Serb offensive, can you just discuss what's stated in the article and whether the article seems accurate to you in light of your review of the other documents we've been talking about.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This does seem to match the descriptions that were given in the ECMM and in the VJ documentation and the other documentation reviewed for the report, a general description of the conflict in Kosovo during this period and some of the specifics such as the attack on the Belacevac village area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It states on the first page, about halfway down: "The Serbs believe this is the final military offensive, a Western military observer said, but this is the third attempt since March by the Serbian security Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. forces to wipe out the rebels. Each attempt has only brought an escalation of the fighting and so will this one." And I think you've already discussed it, but did the intensity of the fighting escalate after the end of June?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes. According to the reports, particularly VJ reports, the intensity did pick up in July when they -- and it's mentioned in the Joint Command minutes that they were conducting a multi-phase operation at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Skipping one paragraph and going to the next: "At a Serbian police checkpoint about a mile outside Lapusnik, a hamlet a mile south of Negrovce, houses were alight and explosions could be heard. A barricade of cars and cement blocks at Lapusnik manned by rebel fighters with rocket-propelled grenades blocks the road to Pec and has cut off the Serb-held town of Kijevo for seven weeks." Now, again, fairly self-evident but can you comment on the level of intensity of the combat appears to be at this time and the weaponry reported to be used by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: There's references to a rocket-propelled grenade in the previous paragraph, armoured vehicles and mortar rounds being used, but in order to hold a town for several weeks, as described here, it would presume that the KLA was fairly well -- well-armed and well able to put up fairly strong defensive operations in the face of a much stronger Serbian force. This wasn't the information on this -- on this conflict from this news report but more importantly from all the other reports reviewed from my report suggests that the KLA was managing to hold territory and that requires holding positions and staying in fairly static positions at times. So they weren't just conducting hit-and-run operations and disappearing back into the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm now going to ask you to look at and discuss some documents relevant to combat operations in July. The first one is at tab 29, 03060823. This is a report dated the 7th of August, but it's reporting on actions between 25th July and the 6th of August, 1998. There are other VJ documents for earlier times in July in annex B but we're not going to go over all of those. Which unit is this report from and which -- and to whom is it being reported?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: This is the 15th Armoured Brigade reporting to the Pristina Corps. The 15th Armoured Brigade was one of the four active combat arms brigades in the Pristina Corps, and the other three active brigades submitted the same reports at roughly the same time, and comments on activities -- combat activities conducted by sub-units of that brigade during a specific period, which was the 25th of July to the 6th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is it routine to have brigades submit reports after major offences or operations?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, this is routine reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The first paragraph talks about between July -- 25th July and 6 August 1998, MUP units being engaged by a decision of the Joint Command along the following axis including Lapusnik village. It then goes in the second paragraph to state: "The MUP forces engaged consisted of the 1st and 2nd MUP detachments, the SAJ unit, and the Brazil unit." Can you talk about -- you've already talked about how the Joint Command brought together the military and the MUP in operations, but what types of MUP units were these that are being engaged along with VJ units?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: These are the special MUP units, the ones that are trained for and equipped for combat operations. The reference to detachments is a reference to the PJP, and a detachment would be roughly 200 or more personnel. So there's two of those in this paragraph. And the special Anti-Terrorist Unit was the more elite, smaller unit. The Brazil unit is -- Brazil is a nickname for the Special Operations Unit, the JSO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And typically if you can take these units by turn, SAJ, JSO, how would they be armed? What weaponry would they have at their disposal at this time?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: They'd each -- each member would have a personal weapon which would be an automatic rifle. Some would have machine-guns, medium and heavy machine-guns. They would also have mortars including up to 120-millimetre mortars. And they also made use of air defence artillery systems which were mounted on vehicles. But the air defence artillery systems are, to describe them roughly, very heavy machine-guns which you would use typically to shoot down aircraft but can be used against ground targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then in paragraph 2, in the middle, it talks -- the report describes the weapons used by what are called the separatists, the KLA, during this offensive, and the local features adapted for firing from. Can you just describe what these weapons are for our benefit, 60-millimetre and 82-millimetre mortars, and the description of bunkers, fortified buildings, trenches, and so on.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: A 60-millimetre mortar is quite a small mortar that is issued at the sub-unit level, but more importantly, the 82-millimetre mortar is a mortar that launches a projectile, and the projectile can be an explosive shell typically, and the use of such systems requires a fair amount of training in order for the projectile to hit the desired target. The references to fortified buildings, trenches and other features suggests that the KLA had dug in and had been prepared to conduct a defensive operation from a static position using heavy weapons. They weren't just intending to conduct a typical terrorist attack of shooting an individual or ambushing one vehicle and leaving the scene immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I think it's pretty clear from your description, but these are not evenly matched forces, are they?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: No. The Serb forces vastly outnumbered the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you could look at tab 30 now, 03078583, 8th of August, again to the Pristina Corps command. We just looked at the 15th Armoured Brigade. This is the 549th Motorised Brigade report for the period -- a little bit greater period, 18 July through 16th of August. So can you tell us what this separate brigade is reporting to the Pristina command?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: This brigade's reporting a similar thing to the 15th Armoured Brigade, which is that it conducted combat operations with the MUP between 18 July and 6 August, at least. At least, that was the period that the Pristina Corps had asked hem to report on. The Prizren Brigade, or the 549 Brigade is headquartered in Prizren and covers an area extending to Djakovica and Orahovac and further on down to the Macedonian and Albanian borders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: About the middle -- well, below the middle of the page, the report states: "Our combat group that was engaged comprised command communications squad, reconnaissance platoon, Military Police Platoon, M-83 armoured combat vehicle platoon, tank platoon, 30/2 millimetre Pat anti-aircraft tank, and a 122-millimetre howitzer platoon and a logistics squad." Some of these weapons described are different from in the previous document. If you can, can you just tell us what types of weapons these are and how they're used in combat.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: They're all what would be termed heavy weapon systems. They come from components of the brigade which are brought together to form a combat group on a temporary basis. So units, sections, for example, of an infantry battalion and the tank battalion which formed part of the brigade would be taken and put together to form the combat group. They had tanks. It doesn't say what type of tank, but they did have the T-55 tank which would use its -- its main gun probably against bunkers and fortified positions. The howitzer platoon, that's an artillery unit which would have six guns, and the platoon -- the howitzer would typically be deployed up to about ten kilometres away from the target. It's hard to say in Kosovo but it could be deployed ten kilometres from the target or further, and lob artillery shells at specific targets. Sometimes it could be used in the direct-fire role where it's pointed from a close distance directly at a target and it could be used against, again, fortified positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And just looking at this for a minute, it talks about different units of this brigade, different SAJ units, MUP units. If you can tell, approximately how many men are involved in the combat operations described in this report? Take a moment to look at it if you need to.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Very roughly, it's -- it's close to 500 personnel or more. It depends on how many they were putting into a MUP detachment. A company of PJP would have about 120 to 150 people, and a detachment would consist of about anywhere from four to seven companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can now look at the report for this same time frame essentially now from the 125th Brigade for the period July 25th to the 6th of August. It's at tab 31. 03077366. Another brigade reporting. There are many references here to PJP detachments. I won't ask you to go through all of the different armaments again, but can you comment on what's reflected in this report on the actions of their brigade and the MUP units during the July offensive.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: This -- this shows that the 125th Brigade was essentially conducting the same combat operations as the other brigades mentioned. It's -- but in its own area of responsibility, which covered pretty much Northern Kosovo extending from the western border across to the Serbia proper. It shows the brigade operating in conjunction with the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I neglected to exhibit the New York Times article. I'm not sure if I did. That was behind tab 47. I'd like to make that exhibit. It's not included in the report. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Tab 47 will be received. Or just a moment. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: As one federal judge once said to me, "All the news that fits, we print," and on that basis we're happy to have the masthead of the New York Times received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 47 will be Prosecution Exhibit P233.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise for having to come back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We can go through this next document at tab 32 quite quickly. This is L 0105347, report from the 8th of August, 243rd Mechanised Brigade to the Pristina Corps PRK command. Again, 25th July to the 7th of August. I'm most interested, I suppose, in section C. If you can tell us what this means: "BG-3 operated independently and did not cooperate with MUP forces. "VJ hardware was used in full accordance with the rules of combat. It was fired only in cases of extreme necessity at shelters, routes, bunkers and fortified elements of the Siptar terrorists. "Combat vehicles were escorted and guarded by infantry with artillery fire support." That's, I guess, fairly self-evident, but could you translate it for us.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: One of the combat groups formed by this brigade obviously didn't conduct operations jointly with the MUP during this period, and it Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. describes using its own infantry to conduct some operations, and it's fairly routine to protect armoured vehicles and artillery with infantry. It describes using artillery to support the operations, which is fairly significant because artillery is -- has a fairly devastating effect and would be used against targets that are representing a fairly serious threat and typically static targets. So it could be possible that the VJ -- that the KLA was dug in into defensive positions and artillery used against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: The reference to rules of combat was they were given rules of engagement and they say they adhered to those.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then they continue in 2 and 3 to claim that they behaved properly during these operations. If we could jump back to tab 21, KLA communique number 49. This is previously exhibited as P048, Your Honours. This is from the 12th of July, and the communique states: "... the struggle in Kosova between the KLA and the invading Serbian military and police forces has assumed wider operational dimensions. KLA units are harvesting considerable successes, bringing under control and retaining many strategically --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: " ... and facilities of vital importance for Kosova's future." And then it goes on to talk about measures against collaborators. Can you just comment on the credibility of that report in light of the VJ and ECMM documents which we've reviewed for July?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: This communique corroborates the other sources that I referred to in my report. The descriptions of an intensification in the extent of operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to now look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before you do, is that a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you give an indication of how much longer you'd expect to be in chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm pretty close to finished. I'm just going to go through a few more documents, ECMM and KDOM, for July. I'll definitely finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We'll finish July soon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Again, if it's of any assistance to anybody, we do agree those documents, for the purposes of which they've been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will resume at five minutes to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just to be clear, the Defence did agree for the report and the supporting material to be exhibited. I thank them for that. They would not agree that the report could come in without cross-examination. That's why we're having a direct as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Coo, I'm almost done. I want to now look at a few ECMM KDOM reports for July. The first one is at tab 35, 26 July, R025-4238. Under the General heading, this document talks about the Serb offensive of late July, beginning 24th of July, and describes the main objective being the retaking of the main road west from Pristina to Pec. Under Security, similar information. " ... it appears that the main aim of the security forces is the retaking of the main road west from Pristina to Pec with the KLA security force clashes in the area of Lapusnik west of the security checkpoint at Komorane and an area east of Klina close to the security checkpoint in Kijevo." Does this corroborate and fit with the brigade reports which we've reviewed to the -- to their command for the period 26 July through August?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, it does, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The next tab, 36. This is a KDOM weekly report from 20th to 26th July, 1998, R025-3670. And the first page KDOM talks about significant observations and events. First situation, the town of Orahovac is under control of the security forces following KLA action. This action began just prior to the reporting period. So that would be talking about the action being just prior to the 20th of July; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if we look at section B, which is on -- it's not numbered, but the fourth page, "Freedom of movement/access." And just to be clear, when people are reading these documents, FOM stands for "freedom of movement" wherever we see that, and FOA "freedom of access"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Zone B: "On 20th of July a team of Russian state television were detained in the area of Lapusnik by the UCK for 5 hours and threatened with weapons. Their Albanian interpreter was beaten and his fate remains unknown." That's again corroborative, is it not, of the VJ documents we've looked at which talk about KLA kidnappings?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we look at tab 38 -- excuse me, 37. R026-0854. Now an ECMM document from 27 July 1998. Taken as a whole, this document provides evidence and corroborates the existence of armed combat in the Lapusnik area prior to the 27th of July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Tab --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the remaining documents I would have gone through are not contained in the report. These are documents at tabs 39 through 46. They are all EU KDOM or ECMM reports. During the break, my colleagues have agreed to admit these documents without going through the process of discussing them with the witness, so these will need to be assigned exhibit numbers, if we could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Let's identify each one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. Tab 39 is R025-3666 through 3667.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 39 will be Prosecution Exhibit P234.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: At tab 40, R025-4248. It's a 20th of July report by KDOM.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 40 will be Prosecution Exhibit P235.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: At tab 41, R025-6005, another 20th of July report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 41 will be Prosecution Exhibit P236.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 42 will be Prosecution Exhibit P237.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 43 will be Prosecution Exhibit P238.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Number 44 we have R025-4247.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 44 will be Prosecution Exhibit P239.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 45 will be Prosecution Exhibit P240.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 46 will be Prosecution Exhibit P241.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Coo. I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Coo. My name is Richard Harvey, and together with my learned friend Mr. Gregor Guy-Smith we represent Mr. Bala, who sits in the middle behind us. Just so you understand, there may be one or two questions that others of my colleagues may have, but I'm essentially here as part of a collective to ask you some questions based on your work as an analyst in this case. You follow me so far?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a little bit about how you do your job. You did say in answer to Mr. Nicholls at the beginning of your testimony that you focus on the conflicts pertaining to Kosovo primarily connected to the Serb accused that we have indicted. I noted particularly your use of the expression "that we have indicted." Now, you are part of a Prosecution team, essentially, here; correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And your function now is as the head of the military analysis team. "MAT" is being whispered in my ear by Mr. Khan who understands these acronyms better than I do. So you're head of the MAT; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: How many people work under you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: There's a total of 18 people, 14 of whom are analysts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And is part of your task concerned with researching in order to see whether indictments should be preferred and another part of it concerned with researching after indictments have been brought in order to find evidence in support of the indictments?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: We -- the MAT does generally support the Prosecution teams in efforts to draft indictments, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Well, you're involved in the pre-indictment phase in providing information that may lead to the bringing of an indictment; correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And are you also involved post-indictment in looking for further and additional material that may help support the indictment that's already been brought?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, we are. We examine all the material that we think is of relevance to the conflict, we don't just look at the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Right. The focus of your expertise is primarily on the command, control, structure, and operation of the FRY and Serb forces. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes. That's been the bulk of my work at the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And you testified some little time ago in the trial of Mr. Milosevic, did you not?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Which year was that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That was in -- it's my recollection it was September 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And up until that time you had not been tasked with looking into Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the command structure of the KLA at all, had you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I hadn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: When were you first tasked with that duty?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I've never been tasked with looking at the command structure of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You were brought in in the Milosevic case to analyse the extent to which it can fairly be said that he, Mr. Milosevic, had direct command responsibility for the VJ, the MUP, and their operations in Kosovo. Is that at least part of your responsibility in that case?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: The task I was given was more general. It was to assess the information that we had that would describe how the armed groups in Kosovo, the Serb armed groups, were structured, commanded, and controlled.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And obviously the relationship of that structure command and control to the head of state in the person of Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: To some degree, yes. There's another team within the Office of the Prosecutor called the leadership research team which analyses more of the political issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: At that stage, you were concerned primarily with the Milosevic indictment period which is all concerned with 1999. At least, none of it is concerned with 1998; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: The indictment is solely 1999, but a great deal of work was conducted reviewing documentation from 1998 and prior to that, and that was necessary to -- to describe the -- the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: To find out -- essentially, to establish how things had deteriorated to the point where they had in 1999, you had to look back to 1998?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That was one aspect but also to describe the way the Serb forces were structured, commanded, and controlled required analysis of documents from 1998 and prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You looked into how the VJ and MUP conducted psychological operations.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't focus on psychological operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Did you focus on any of the paramilitary groups associated with or sponsored by VJ and MUP?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I didn't focus on paramilitary groups either, with the exception of an attempt to determine whether or not those groups fell under the command or control of the VJ MUP or any other Serb command structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Did you attempt to discover whether the -- the Black Hand group fell under the SAJ or any of the other -- JSO or any of the other acronyms of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: What paramilitary groups did you investigate?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: No paramilitary group by particular name. There -- the purpose of my analysis of what paramilitary groups -- of the involvement of paramilitary groups was limited to determining whether or not the paramilitary groups fell under the official chains of command. I didn't have the information I needed. Some of the information was also in witness statements or witness testimony, which I couldn't use, so the scope of my report was limited to the information I had, which was to -- which allowed me to determine whether or not those paramilitary groups fell within an official chain of command. And the outcome of the analysis was that it was assessed that the official chains of command did not tolerate paramilitary groups operating in a rogue fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: That, of course -- you're familiar with the concept of plausible deniability, I assume.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I've heard it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: When you say they did not tolerate it, officially, I think you qualified that with. Unofficially was there toleration, as far as you were able to establish, of the activities of paramilitary groups?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I couldn't establish that because the information I had didn't describe the activities of the paramilitary groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: But that you did establish that there were paramilitary groups that did appear to be operating in a rogue fashion, as you described it.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: The -- to clarify what I said, the paramilitary groups, the existence of paramilitary groups in Kosovo in 1999 and prior to that wasn't tolerated according to the information that I was reviewing. For example, there was an order from the MUP in, I think, 1997 or 1998 saying that they were to take action against information they were acquiring that paramilitary groups were attempting to move into Kosovo in 1998. So I had no information that I could use in my report. As I said, the information was in witness statements. I had no information for my report on the activities of the paramilitary groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Are we right to assume that when you're speaking of paramilitary groups in this context, you're referring to paramilitary groups that would be hostile to ethnic Albanians in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And there were such groups at the time period we're talking of in 1998 that did appear to be operating in Kosovo in a rogue fashion?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I have come across information that does suggest that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Because one of the matters that was of proper concern to you, if I may suggest, was the extent to which weapons were being distributed in a wholesale fashion to civilians under the orders of the VJ and the MUP.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's correct. I was reviewing information on that. And, Your Honours, I should clarify my response, earlier response was that I was generally aware from what information I'd read that rogue group -- that the KLA -- sorry, that paramilitary groups were operating in Kosovo in 1998. Whether they were operating in a rogue fashion outside an official chain of command, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You came across no evidence that linked the paramilitary groups in an official, non-rogue fashion into the structure of the VJ or MUP, if I understand you correctly.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: In addition to the questions of paramilitary activities and the questions of distribution of weapons to civilians, you were concerned in general to investigate patterns and practices of violations of international humanitarian law by the VJ and the MUP.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That wasn't in the remit of my report, and it's not within my expertise to determine whether or not there were violations of international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: It was within your remit to determine whether they appeared to have been operating in violation of their own constitution.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: It was with respect to their chain of command as described in the -- their -- their constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Because if I've understood your evidence correctly, it appears that throughout the period that we're looking at, which is 1998 up until the end of July, throughout that period the VJ was operating on a systematic and consistently illegal basis under the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, I don't think I've come to that conclusion anywhere. I report that, for example, General Perisic, the chief of the General Staff at that time, felt that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: He might be thought to be somebody who would have a little bit of an understanding of that situation?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: He would be, but we've received so much conflicting information on that it seems to be a very complex legal issue from the perspective of FRY law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: So it's not for -- I couldn't determine within my expertise whether they violated that law or constitution or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Certainly you have the general who has overall responsibility for the operation of FRY in Kosovo raising this spectre of wholesale illegality; correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's correct. I wouldn't regard it as wholesale illegality. They were primarily operating in the border areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And secondly, apart from the VJ, the MUP also appeared to have been operating in an illegal fashion under the Yugoslav constitution.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: From my understanding, it's not actually the constitution but it's the law on defence in this case which says that during a state of emergency or other extraordinary state the MUP can be subordinated to the VJ for combat operations, but that law and nothing I have seen rules out the MUP operating in combat roles outside of those extraordinary states. It may be the case, but I haven't seen anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Well, again, we're going to look at them as we go along, but you did come across documents which indicated serious concern by generals that MUP was operating illegally and being used for illegal purposes by civilians who had no business operating in that fashion.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's General Perisic's opinion of the way the Joint Command was working.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Do you have an opinion that General Perisic had -- had completely lost his mind about this, or does it appear to be a genuine concern?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: In my assessment, General Perisic had reasonable concerns that the VJ was operating without the formal procedures that would normally be gone through in the political system in the FRY at that time. That may be the way Milosevic operated. There may be other reasons. I just -- I'm not an expert on FRY law or the FRY constitution to be able to make a determination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. I'm going to be asking you a number of questions arising out of your testimony during the Milosevic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And for that purpose we have prepared, Your Honours -- we have a copy of the entire testimony of the witness. I don't think it should be necessary to worry you with that. We have selected out the pages to which we will be referring, and the testimony took place, I think, on the 11th of September of 2002, if I recall correctly. So if those copies could be given to the usher. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters please have a copy also.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'll try not to jump about too much with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, we'll wait to try and ensure the interpreters get a copy, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There was a cry for help.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just ask Your Honours, no objection, but if the witness feels he wants to look at other parts of his testimony, in that case that be made available for him if he needs -- needs it to complete his answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Most certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps we can wait and see if it becomes relevant, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yes. We have it here if need be. Everybody has it, I understand, now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Coo, just to reiterate what His Honour Judge Parker just said, we have the full copy here at any time you want to refer to it, okay?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: The first thing I want to start with, if I may, is page 9992, at Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. line 18, which is on the third page of the transcript we have here. And that continuing on until 9993, line 12. I just want to ask you a little bit about the forces which operated under the Special Operations Unit, and essentially focusing from line 1 of page 9993. The MUP refers to "... the state security division responsible for, in very general terms, counter-intelligence. It also had a special arm -- heavily armed uniformed unit called the Special Operations Unit, or the JSO, sometimes known by the unofficial term 'Red Berets' or 'Frenki's Boys.'" We'll come back to the SAJ in more detail later. Just want to ask you, in relation to Frenki's Boys, that relates to Frenki Simatovic of the JSO?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And that --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. It relates to Frenki Simatovic. Whether it's Frenki Simatovic of the JSO isn't clear. He had a role within the ministry, a department within the ministry. I'm not sure whether he was a member of the JSO or not. I don't think he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Who were Frenki's Boys, then?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: The JSO was the special unit within the Serbian MUP, the division of the Serbian MUP known as the state security service. It was very much like the SAJ in that it was an elite unit. It was heavily armed. They wore combat uniforms similar to uniforms worn by the US; green camouflage uniforms. They had armoured vehicles and heavy weapons. If you saw them, the uninformed observer might mistake them for a military unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Nothing from their appearance certainly to distinguish them from an army military unit?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: There is. The uniforms are different and the insignia are different.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: But if you're on the receiving end of them, the result would be the same.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: It would.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: The unit was notorious, was it not, for carrying out serious human rights violations?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I've obviously read about those allegations but there is nothing that I came across that I could support them with so I didn't cover that in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Was part of your research and background reading the book by Tim Judah, Kosovo: War and Revenge?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I read that book from general knowledge -- out of general interest, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Do you recall a passage in that book where he describes an attack by Frenki's Boys in Decani on a van carrying workers from a nearby power plant where they were ambushed and killed by men wearing black? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I don't recall that. I would be inclined to be skeptical unless I knew how it was determined that they were Frenki's Boys or the JSO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Perhaps we can provide some enlightenment at a later stage on that. The point being that the JSO did carry out attacks that were designed to appear to have been conducted by the KLA in order to discredit the KLA. Would you agree that that did happen?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I can't agree. I've seen nothing that would allow me to agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You've seen nothing at all?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'll take you, then, to the subject of the arming of civilians. This was planned at least as early as May of 1998. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: It was ordered no later than June of 1998, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And the order was that it was to be executed, completed by the 1st of July, 1998. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's correct, according to the document I reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You've already described that to some extent. I'd like you to look, if you would, please, at page 9997, line 24 -- which I clearly don't mean, do I. I mean 9996, line 24, which actually exists. Here you were being asked by Mr. Nice on behalf of the Prosecution in the Milosevic case about your use of the word "saturated," and it reads: "You used the word 'saturated' saying that the local defence concept ensured that Kosovo was saturated with armed organisations. In the same paragraph you conclude that the concept involved brought FRY and Serb forces together in composite units acting ultimately on the authority of the president." You're asked what you meant by "saturated," and you give this answer: "That term is intended to emphasise that not only in Kosovo was defence a responsibility of the regular army, the VJ, and to a large extent also the combat units of the MUP, but there was also, complementing that and taking away some of the load of defending towns and villages, a well-organised system of local defence, and that system was integrated within the federal system of command which I've described elsewhere in the documentation ..." Now, I'd just like to ask you, and please if you want to read on just to the bottom of that page, I don't think I need to read it aloud. Just so you have the full flavour of your answer. The local defence concept is not something that you as a professional military man would endorse. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: No, it's not fair to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: It's not fair to say that? I'm sorry, you wouldn't endorse it or it's not fair to say that you wouldn't endorse it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I can't -- I wouldn't not endorse it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: As practised by VJ and MUP, would you endorse that practice?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I guess --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to object on vagueness. I don't know what counsel means by "endorse the practice." Maybe if it could be asked a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm happy to become a little more specific about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: This local defence concept meant that Kosovo was saturated by weapons in the hands of FRY, the Serb forces, and those civilians whom they trusted only; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Partially correct. And I should say that I can't comment on the extent to which the local defence concept was in effect in 1998. There was certainly orders to bring it into effect and to identify people to whom arms should be given, and there was the Joint Command instruction from July explaining in great detail how the concept should be set up. There are some references from documents in my report suggesting that they -- they were functioning, but the extent to which they were in 1998, I don't know. The reference to civilians, there were in fact other elements to civilian defence, and those -- to local defence, and that was a civilian defence structure which was an official Ministry of Defence structure intended to, as I said earlier, to protect vital installations, among other things. There were provisions in the law to arm them. They received training, and they had official chains of command. There were documents that I saw that suggested that in addition to these official organisations, they were arming civilians, but those civilians were being trained and integrated into an official chain of command. They were always with, to my knowledge, civilian defence, MUP, and possibly VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: We're putting an awful lot of faith here on documents produced by the VJ, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Those documents, most of which are corroborated by other documents, at least, in this -- the report for this case, not all of the documents on local defence were produced by the VJ. The means by which we got the documents vary quite widely, so I tended to afford them some reliability.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Could we have a look -- there's a document which I've asked to be copied and circulated. It's K number is K022-7997. And the translation is at 03078003. If that could be circulated. Thank you. The advantage of the distribution process is it gives all of us a chance to have a look at it, Mr. Coo. This is the order sent by General Pavkovic on the 26th of June, 1998, on distributing weapons, among others, to the civilian population; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I just have to have a quick review of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't hear what you said.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Sorry. I just have to review it quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I see now. Paragraph 8 specifically refers to: "I forbid formation and engagement of any volunteer units except those comprising local village inhabitants."

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's correct. I just don't see any reference specifically to the distribution of weapons to civilians. It does suggest that civilians will be involved in local defence, but I don't see the specific reference like paragraph 1 to weapons going to civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: We'll probably come to that fairly soon anyway. By the way, reference here is made to military conscripts. Are you aware of the extent to which military service had operated in Kosovo up to and including 1998?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Not in detail. I'm aware that there was an obligation under the law for able-bodied men between the ages of, I think, 18 and 65 or 55 to do their national service. I understood that a lot of the Kosovo Albanians didn't complete that service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: But by contrast, a lot of ethnic Serbs and non-Kosovan Albanians did complete their service; correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Correct. I'm not ruling out that the Kosovo Albanians did get military service. A lot of them had it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: We've heard already that some certainly did. But it was easy, therefore, for the army command to call back those who had already done their service, and they knew because of their records whom they could trust, or who they at least thought they could trust with weapons. Do you think that's a fair observation?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: But this order of the 26th of June requires that weapons be distributed to military conscripts, in paragraph 1, that it be done in security and secrecy. And paragraph 3: "On the basis of the lists, call up military transcripts [sic] in small groups to the army barracks --" Did I say "transcripts"? "... military conscripts in small groups to the army barracks for organised distribution and issue of weapons in Serbian and Montenegrin villages. Devote special attention to security measures, secrecy and camouflage discipline in carrying out this task." So great care is being taken to arm one section of the population effectively against another section of that population, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's correct, and I had that in my report for the Milosevic trial. There were indications that they -- there were also loyal Albanians armed in parts of -- in some local defence units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Generally speaking, when Albanians did their military service, is it correct to say that they were assigned to non-combat roles? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I don't have enough to say anything conclusive about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Anyway, we see on -- at paragraph 10 on the second page that: "The deadline for the distribution of these weapons is until 1800 hours on the 1st of July 1998 ..." So four days, they've got to get all these weapons out there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Which suggests, would you agree, that preparations would already have been well advanced once -- for the -- to be ready to go as soon as the order was given.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'd just like to look with you, if I may, at your testimony at pages 10010, starting at line 22. This refers, I believe, to tab 6 of your report, the order from Petar Ilic, chief of defence administration, that chiefs of departments and heads of sections shall immediately establish contacts with municipal leaders and ensure that lists are compiled for the purpose of arming of the population. And that's an order dated the 21st of May, as we've -- as you've already said in chief; right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: So you would agree that that order of the 21st of May signals the preparation for the order that is going to come on the 26th of June that is going to be completed by the 1st of July, arming specific sections of the population against other sections of the population.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: We discussed the same subject. I can't say whether the July ones or the June ones are a direct outcome of the May one, but there is a connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Then in relation to tab 8, I'd just like to ask you a couple of questions. This is the dramatic warning letter from General Pavkovic to the collegium of 3rd Army commanders. Would you look with me, please, at page 10023, point 11, which refers to this letter. It says in terms, looking at line 11: "Despite the arming of the population, that factor in the system against terrorist struggle has not been included." That is the -- that is the arming of the population has not been included in the resistance to the terrorist struggle. Do you follow me?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: When you testified later at a hundred -- 10094, lines 6 through 11, you said at line 11 --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I'm not sure I have 10094.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. 10094.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Mine jumps from 10088 to 10103.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Then -- you're quite right. It's my error. I had not asked for that page to be copied. May I just ask you this and see if you accept it. Otherwise, I'll get the full reference for you. You referred to this letter --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have page 10094 here if you want to show it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed. We have the full transcript anyway, don't we. Where is the full transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It would suit me personally to break a little early. I don't want to do that if you're at a point where the flow would be disturbed, but in view of the need to sort out the right page, I raise it in case this would be a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Then I think my convenience and yours coincide, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will resume tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
